description: From the United States to India, and across Europe, populist leaders are shaking up the traditional parties. Why is this wave hitting **almost every democracy** at the same time?

hero.hook: The people against the elites: a pitch more than a century old, and never more convincing than now.

blocks.text: Since the 2010s, **populism** has no longer been a fringe phenomenon. From the United States to India, and across Europe and Latin America, leaders are shaking up parties that had held power for decades.
The movement did not come out of nowhere. It grows out of very real economic, cultural and technological cracks. This course looks at the logic of that message and at the reasons for its rise.

Populism is not defined by a precise economic program, but by a very particular political logic. For the political scientist Jan-Werner Müller, its central idea is [[monism]]: there is only one “real people,” and the populist leader is its only spokesman.

blocks.caption: Populist rhetoric splits society into two opposing camps

blocks.text: That view divides society in two. On one side, a “pure people” who carry authentic values. On the other, a “corrupt elite” accused of betraying the common good. The frame is very flexible. On the right, the people are usually defined by the nation, against an elite judged too globalist. On the left, they are defined by social class, against a financial elite.

The very first big modern populist party, the American People's Party of 1892, already demanded that the railroads be nationalized, because farmers believed an invisible financial elite was setting the rates.

sections.title: The pure people against the corrupt elite

blocks.text: Several crises came together to explain the rise. On the economic side, the researcher Branko Milanović showed that between 1988 and 2008 the Asian middle classes and the richest people in the world saw their incomes climb, while Western middle classes stagnated. That feeling of sliding down the ladder fed a lasting anger.

blocks.caption: The migration crisis of 2015 fed a sense of identity insecurity in Europe

blocks.text: On top of that economic split came a cultural one. The pace of social change and the migration crisis of 2015 created an identity insecurity for many voters, who feel further and further from the decisions taken by urban elites.

Finally, social media transformed political communication. It sharpens polarization and lets leaders speak straight to their audience, in simple and emotional language, without going through the traditional press.

Populist figures come in many shapes. Donald Trump reshaped the American Republican Party around protectionism and nationalism. In Hungary, Viktor Orbán built the model he himself calls [[Illiberal democracies]], where the result of an election justifies an ever-greater concentration of power.

blocks.caption: Very different figures share the same rhetoric of rupture with the elites

blocks.text: In France, Marine Le Pen ran a strategy of [[normalization]] to widen her electorate, while keeping a message built on national preference. Left-wing populism, embodied by Jean-Luc Mélenchon in France or Bernie Sanders in the United States, puts the redistribution of wealth first, but shares the same rhetoric of breaking with the “system.”

The great paradox of populism appears once it wins. The leader can no longer simply oppose the system: he becomes the system. To keep his rebel image, he often names new enemies, judges or civil servants, accused of blocking his will.

That is where the risk to institutions becomes concrete. In Hungary and in Poland, reforms have aimed at reducing the independence of the courts. After an electoral defeat, some leaders even challenge the legitimacy of the vote, as during the attack on the Capitol in 2021.

One of the most popular presidents in American history, Andrew Jackson, was nicknamed “King Mob” by his critics, because he opened the White House to the public for a party that ended in something close to a riot.
But the rise also works as a useful alarm bell: it forces traditional parties to take up neglected subjects, such as industrial sovereignty or public services in rural areas.

Populism splits the world into a “pure people” against a “corrupt elite.” It has been rising everywhere since 2010, carried by the inequalities of globalization and by a cultural insecurity that social media amplifies.

subtitle: Since the 2010s
title: Populism: why is it rising everywhere?
